I'm Keerthana, Zainab's roommate. When her mother fell ill in August, Zainab said it would be a few weeks. By October it clearly wasn't. She was taking the night bus home every Friday and coming back on Monday grey-faced, and she'd missed two quizzes.
One evening she came back from the academic adviser's office with a stapled sheet. She sat on her bed and read it out to me. "Drop two of my five courses this term. Take them next year. Keep the three I can manage from home on weekends." At the bottom there was a line: "Return to full load: January, review with adviser in December."
She didn't cry, which surprised me. She looked almost lighter, though I can't say what she felt. That week she went home on Thursday instead of Friday and came back with her notes actually finished.

Week one of November. Varun had told everyone his father would be back on his feet by Diwali. He wasn't. Varun was failing two midterms and had started skipping labs to drive his father to appointments in the next town.
Week two. His friend Pranav walked him to the student adviser's office. "Just ask what's possible." The adviser laid out options on a sheet: reduce to two courses, or take the whole term off and return in the next session with his place held. Varun asked for a night to think.
Week three. He chose the term break. He filled in the form, saved the adviser's email with the return date, and made a list of the two courses to retake first. On his last day on campus he returned his library books and told Pranav, "I'm not dropping out. I'm stepping out and coming back." Then he took the bus home.

passage:
Last week I didn't exercise once. Not one day. I'd been going to the football ground at eight in the evening for six weeks, and then everything collapsed.
My first thought was: that's it, I'm not someone who sticks with things. I nearly deleted the tracking sheet.
Instead, my friend Uday made me look at it with him. We scrolled back. Every missed day had the same note: stayed late at work, too tired. The mornings, the few I'd tried, had never been missed.
So I changed two things. Sessions moved to 6:30 a.m. And one rule, written at the top of the sheet: never miss twice in a row. One missed day is life. Two is a new habit.
It's been three weeks. I've missed two single days, never two together. I'm Zainab, and I'm learning that a bad week is information, not a verdict.

qa.q: What time did Zainab move the sessions to?
qa.a: Zainab moved them to 6:30 a.m.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel after the missed week, before looking at the sheet?
qa.a: Zainab felt discouraged and like a failure, thinking of being someone who doesn't stick with things and nearly deleting the sheet.

qa.q: What else could Zainab track to keep adjusting?
qa.a: Zainab could note energy levels on morning sessions, so if mornings start failing too, the next change is based on data.

qa.q: How might Uday feel after helping Zainab look at the sheet?
qa.a: Uday may feel glad and a bit proud that looking back at the notes helped Zainab keep going instead of quitting.

grounding: Shows the person treating a missed week as data, moving sessions from evenings to mornings and adding a never-miss-twice rule.

subtype: Approach: track and adjust after a missed week [Revision]
passage:
Coach's note, community sports centre, week 10. Written by Ira.
Tarun missed all three of his sessions last week, and I half expected he'd drop out, as many do after a gap. Instead he came in on Monday with his phone open to the log he keeps.
He had already worked it out. "Every session I missed was at seven in the evening. I haven't missed one morning in two months," he said. "So I want to switch to the 6 a.m. group."
He also showed me a line he had added at the top of his log: "Never miss twice in a row." When I asked about it, he said, "One gap is fine. Two and I'm back to zero."
He seemed a bit sheepish about the week, but not defeated.
Next step: I moved him to the morning group and asked him to show me the log again at the end of the month.

qa.q: Which group did Tarun ask to switch to?
qa.a: He asked to switch to the 6 a.m. group.

qa.q: How did Tarun seem to feel about the missed week?
qa.a: He seemed a bit sheepish about it, but not defeated.

qa.q: What else could Tarun do if mornings start slipping too?
qa.a: He could look at his log again to see what changed, since he already uses it to spot patterns instead of giving up.

qa.q: How does Tarun's approach look to the coach?
qa.a: The coach expected him to drop out, so seeing him arrive with a plan from his log is a pleasant surprise worth supporting.

grounding: Shows the person, after a missed week, spotting that evening sessions fail, moving to mornings and adding a never-miss-twice rule.
